title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 17-24
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 17-24 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Large Data Volumes: Archiving, Big Objects, Skinny Tables, and Indexing Strategy”, what is the central focus?
options: How an org stays fast and inside its storage as volume grows: selectivity and custom indexes, skinny tables for read-heavy hot data, big objects for bulk historical storage, and archiving as the tier that sheds cold data before it drags everything down.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: How an org stays fast and inside its storage as volume grows: selectivity and custom indexes, skinny tables for read-heavy hot data, big objects for bulk historical storage, and archiving as the tier that sheds cold data before it drags everything down.

questions.explanation: Lesson 16 ended with data finally loaded into the org.

questions.question: Per the lesson “System Limits: Governor, API, and Storage Limits, and Planning Around Them”, what is the central focus?
options: Governors exist to keep a multitenant platform fair. Learn the limits, then bulkify, batch, and monitor so they never fire on your watch.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Governors exist to keep a multitenant platform fair. Learn the limits, then bulkify, batch, and monitor so they never fire on your watch.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Every Salesforce org lives inside three sets of constraints: governor limits that cap what a single Apex transaction can do, API request allocations that cap how many external calls an org gets per day, and storage limits that cap how much data and how many files you can keep.

The opposite is true: every Salesforce org lives inside three sets of constraints: governor limits that cap what a single Apex transaction can do, API request allocations that cap how many external calls an org gets per day, and storage limits that cap how much data and how many files you can keep.
The lesson says only technical staff should act on this.
The lesson advises ignoring this entirely in practice.
questions.explanation: Every Salesforce org lives inside three sets of constraints: governor limits that cap what a single Apex transaction can do, API request allocations that cap how many external calls an org gets per day, and storage limits that cap how much data and how many files you can keep.

questions.explanation: The daily total is the sum of a base amount, a per-license contribution, and any purchased add-ons.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Environment and Release Strategy: Sandbox Types, Change Sets vs DevOps (sf/sfdx)”, what is the central focus?
options: Where work happens and how it moves to production. The four sandbox types (Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy, Full), what each copies and how often it refreshes, then the release-mechanism fork: click-based change sets versus source-driven deployment with the sf CLI and a Git-based source of truth, including Salesforce DX and DevOps Center.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Where work happens and how it moves to production. The four sandbox types (Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy, Full), what each copies and how often it refreshes, then the release-mechanism fork: click-based change sets versus source-driven deployment with the sf CLI and a Git-based source of truth, including Salesforce DX and DevOps Center.

questions.explanation: This lesson is about the orgs themselves: where work happens, and how completed work travels from a developer's sandbox to production.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Enterprise gets a Partial Copy but no Full sandbox by default, so a small Enterprise org that needs a staging replica must buy a Full license.
Enterprise gets a Partial Copy but no Full sandbox by default, so a small Enterprise org that needs a staging replica must not buy a Full license.
The lesson says the opposite: this should always be avoided.
The lesson cautions against this in every real-world case.
questions.explanation: Enterprise gets a Partial Copy but no Full sandbox by default, so a small Enterprise org that needs a staging replica must buy a Full license.

questions.question: Per the lesson “General Systems Architecture: Environments and CI/CD in ML and AI Pipelines”, what is the central focus?
options: The same environment-and-release discipline from Lesson 19, applied to machine learning and AI systems.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: The same environment-and-release discipline from Lesson 19, applied to machine learning and AI systems. Why the ML artifact is more than code (code, data, and model all change), the continuous X's (CI, CD, CT, CM), the MLOps maturity levels, how a model promotes from a development environment to production, and what changes when the artifact is a nondeterministic agent that needs eval gates instead of unit tests.
